summary.text: For composite \(n\), an odd prime divisor \(p\mid n\) leaves an extra factor of \(p\) in \(a(n-1)\), by counting the factors \(2^j-1\) with \((p-1)\mid j\) and applying Legendre’s digit-sum formula; this contradicts the hypothesis, while the remaining case \(n=2^k\) is excluded by the exact valuation \(v_2(a(2^k-1))=k-1\). Once \(n\) is prime, if the order \(d\) of \(2\) were less than \(n-1\), then \(n\mid 2^d-1\) would force \(n\mid a(n-1)\) (the factorial denominator is coprime to \(n\)), again contradicting the stated divisibility, so the order is \(n-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N_m=2^{m-1}\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1)\qquad(m\ge 1).
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N_m}{m!}.
\]
We will first establish the divisibility facts that make this quotient integral and then prove the conjecture.

We use the notation \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of a prime \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\), and \(s_p(x)\) for the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(x\). We will repeatedly use Legendre’s digit-sum formula
\[
(p-1)v_p(M!)=M-s_p(M). \tag{1}
\]
In particular, if \(M>0\), then \(s_p(M)\ge 1\), so
\[
(p-1)v_p(M!)\le M-1,
\]
and hence
\[
v_p(M!)\le \left\lfloor\frac{M-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]

### 1. Integrality of the defining quotient

We first prove that
\[
m!\mid N_m \tag{3}
\]
for every \(m\ge1\).

Fix a prime \(p\). If \(p=2\), the initial factor \(2^{m-1}\) in \(N_m\) already contributes \(m-1\) factors of \(2\). By (2),
\[
v_2(m!)\le m-1,
\]
so the power of \(2\) in \(m!\) is no larger than that in \(N_m\).

Now suppose \(p\) is odd, and put
\[
c=\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
For each \(j=1,\dots,c\), the integer
\[
k_j=(p-1)j
\]
satisfies \(1\le k_j\le m-1\). Fermat’s little theorem gives
\[
2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
because \(p\nmid2\). Raising this congruence to the \(j\)-th power shows
\[
p\mid 2^{(p-1)j}-1=2^{k_j}-1.
\]
The \(c\) integers \(k_1,\dots,k_c\) are distinct indices in the product defining \(N_m\). Consequently,
\[
p^c\mid\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1).
\]
By (2), \(v_p(m!)\le c\). Thus the exponent of every odd prime \(p\) in \(m!\) is at most its exponent in \(N_m\). Together with the case \(p=2\), this proves (3). Therefore \(a(m)=N_m/m!\) is indeed an integer, and
\[
N_m=m!a(m). \tag{4}
\]

We next derive two more precise consequences of this argument.

### 2. A sharper valuation for indices one less than a composite multiple of an odd prime

Let \(p\) be prime, let \(t\ge2\), and set
\[
m=pt-1.
\]
We claim that
\[
v_p(m!)+1\le \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{pt-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{5}
\]

To prove this, observe that
\[
pt-1=(p-1)+p(t-1).
\]
This is the base-\(p\) expansion obtained by taking the least significant digit to be \(p-1\) and then appending the base-\(p\) digits of \(t-1\). Since \(t-1>0\), its base-\(p\) digit sum is at least \(1\). Hence
\[
s_p(pt-1)=(p-1)+s_p(t-1)\ge p. \tag{6}
\]
Applying (1) with \(M=pt-1\), we obtain
\[
(p-1)v_p((pt-1)!)
 =pt-1-s_p(pt-1)
 \le pt-1-p.
\]
Adding \(p-1\) to both sides gives
\[
(p-1)\bigl(v_p((pt-1)!)+1\bigr)\le pt-2,
\]
which is exactly (5).

Suppose now that \(p\) is odd. As in the integrality argument, each index
\[
(p-1),2(p-1),\dots,
\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor(p-1)
\]
contributes a factor divisible by \(p\) to \(\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1)\). Thus
\[
v_p(N_m)\ge \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
Combining this with (5) yields
\[
v_p(N_m)\ge v_p(m!)+1.
\]
Because \(m!\mid N_m\), equation (4) and additivity of valuations give
\[
v_p(a(m))=v_p(N_m)-v_p(m!)\ge1.
\]
We have therefore proved the important implication
\[
\boxed{\ p\text{ odd prime},\ t\ge2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\mid a(pt-1).\ } \tag{7}
\]

### 3. The exact power of two at Mersenne indices

We next prove that for every \(r\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{\ v_2\bigl(a(2^r-1)\bigr)=r-1.\ } \tag{8}
\]

Put \(m=2^r-1\). Every factor \(2^k-1\), for \(k\ge1\), is odd. Therefore the complete power of \(2\) in \(N_m\) comes from the factor \(2^{m-1}\), and
\[
v_2(N_m)=m-1. \tag{9}
\]

The binary expansion of \(2^r-1\) consists of exactly \(r\) digits, all equal to \(1\). Thus
\[
s_2(m)=r.
\]
Legendre’s formula (1), with \(p=2\), now gives
\[
v_2(m!)=m-s_2(m)=m-r. \tag{10}
\]
Using \(a(m)=N_m/m!\), equations (9) and (10) imply
\[
v_2(a(m))=(m-1)-(m-r)=r-1,
\]
which proves (8).

We will also use the elementary inequality
\[
2^r\ge r+2\qquad(r\ge2). \tag{11}
\]
It holds at \(r=2\), and induction preserves it because doubling \(2^r\) is at least \((r+1)+2\). In particular,
\[
r\le2^r-2. \tag{12}
\]

### 4. Composite values of \(n\) are impossible

Assume now that \(n>2\) and
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{13}
\]
We prove first that \(n\) is prime.

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(n\) is composite. There are two cases.

#### Case 1: \(n\) is a power of two

Write \(n=2^r\). Since \(n>2\), we have \(r\ge2\). By (12),
\[
2^r\mid 2^{2^r-2}.
\]
On the other hand, (13), after substituting \(n=2^r\), says
\[
2^r\mid a(2^r-1)+2^{2^r-2}.
\]
Subtracting the second summand modulo \(2^r\), we conclude that
\[
2^r\mid a(2^r-1).
\]
This would imply
\[
v_2(a(2^r-1))\ge r,
\]
contradicting the exact valuation (8), which says that this valuation is only \(r-1\). Thus a composite \(n\) satisfying (13) cannot be a power of two.

#### Case 2: \(n\) has an odd prime divisor

If an integer is not a power of two, its odd part is greater than \(1\), and therefore it has an odd prime divisor. Choose such a divisor \(p\), and write
\[
n=pt.
\]
Because we are assuming that \(n\) is composite, \(t\ne1\); also \(t\ne0\) because \(n>2\). Hence \(t\ge2\).

The divisibility (7) gives
\[
p\mid a(pt-1)=a(n-1). \tag{14}
\]
Since \(p\mid n\), hypothesis (13) also gives
\[
p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{15}
\]
Subtracting (14) from (15) modulo \(p\), we get
\[
p\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
This is impossible: \(p\) is odd, so \(p\nmid2\), and consequently no positive power of \(2\) is divisible by \(p\). This eliminates the second case as well.

Every positive integer is either a power of two or has an odd prime divisor, so the two cases exhaust all possibilities. We conclude that
\[
\boxed{n\text{ is prime}.} \tag{16}
\]
Since \(n>2\), this prime is odd.

### 5. Failure of primitivity would force the prime to divide \(a(n-1)\)

We now prove the second part of the conclusion. We first establish a general fact for an odd prime \(p\).

Let \(p>2\) be prime, and suppose that \(2\) is not a primitive root modulo \(p\). Let
\[
d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]
be the multiplicative order of \(2\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times\). Since \(p\nmid2\), this order is positive and divides the order \(p-1\) of the multiplicative group. If \(2\) is not primitive, then \(d\ne p-1\). Therefore
\[
1\le d<p-1. \tag{17}
\]
By the definition of multiplicative order,
\[
2^d\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
so
\[
p\mid2^d-1. \tag{18}
\]

Consider now the numerator for \(a(p-1)\):
\[
N_{p-1}=2^{p-2}\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1).
\]
Condition (17) places \(d\) among the indices \(1,\dots,p-2\). Thus (18) shows that \(p\) divides one factor of this product, and hence
\[
p\mid N_{p-1}. \tag{19}
\]

From the integrality already proved,
\[
N_{p-1}=(p-1)!\,a(p-1). \tag{20}
\]
None of the factors \(1,2,\dots,p-1\) is divisible by \(p\), so
\[
\gcd(p,(p-1)!)=1.
\]
Equations (19) and (20), followed by Euclid’s lemma, therefore imply
\[
\boxed{\ 2\text{ not primitive modulo }p
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\mid a(p-1).\ } \tag{21}
\]

### 6. Completion of the proof

Apply (21) to the prime \(n\) obtained in (16). If \(2\) were not a primitive root modulo \(n\), then
\[
n\mid a(n-1). \tag{22}
\]
But the original hypothesis is
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{23}
\]
Subtracting (22) from (23) modulo \(n\) would give
\[
n\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
This is impossible because \(n>2\) is an odd prime and therefore is coprime to every power of \(2\).

Consequently \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\). Equivalently, its multiplicative order modulo \(n\) is
\[
\varphi(n)=n-1.
\]
Together with (16), this proves that whenever \(n>2\) and
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2},
\]
then \(n\) is prime and \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\), as required.
